name: News-Press & Gazette Company

profile.address: 1623 Farnam, 1623, Farnam Street, Omaha, Douglas County, Nebraska, 68106
profile.reading:
1623 Farnam Street occupies a nine-story, roughly 75,000-square-foot building in downtown Omaha that has operated for more than a decade as one of the Midwest's principal carrier-neutral interconnection hubs rather than as a conventional single-tenant enterprise data center. The facility began as Nebraska Data Centers (NDC), and on November 5, 2018, News-Press & Gazette Company (NPG), a privately held media company based in St. Joseph, Missouri, owned by the Bradley family and best known for newspaper, radio, and television properties across the western United States, acquired NDC and reorganized it as 1623 Farnam, LLC. At acquisition, NPG committed to more than $30 million in capital improvements over the following five years, with the prior NDC leadership, including president Todd Cushing, staying on to run the facility.

That capital commitment has been visible in a steady sequence of expansions: a roughly $10 million buildout in 2019, additional floors brought into service in 2021, and a further expansion completed in June 2025 that added 1.5 megawatts of IT capacity and space for 280 racks across the building's final two data halls, bringing the facility's total capacity to approximately 8 megawatts. In January 2026 the company announced it would add a second Omaha facility to its interconnection campus, extending the carrier-neutral model beyond the original Farnam Street building.

The building's draw for network operators is its interconnection density rather than raw power capacity: 1623 Farnam markets itself as hosting more than 60 network, cloud, content, and wireless carriers, including, by its own account, seven of the world's thirteen largest IP-transit providers, plus direct cloud on-ramps such as Microsoft Azure ExpressRoute and the Omaha IX peering exchange. For power resilience and cooling, the facility draws on Cordia's downtown Omaha district energy system, which the companies describe as providing continuous thermal energy and backup power capability during grid disruptions, an arrangement distinct from the on-site generator plants many suburban data centers rely on instead.

Because the building sits near the geographic middle of the continental United States with access to multiple long-haul fiber routes, 1623 Farnam positions itself as a low-latency hub for coast-to-coast traffic and, more recently, as infrastructure for AI workloads, wireless backhaul, and edge computing. What is not publicly disclosed is a detailed tenant roster, lease terms, or a breakdown of how much of the building's capacity is currently occupied versus available - NPG and 1623 Farnam LLC have published capacity and investment figures at each expansion milestone but have not released standing occupancy or financial data for the facility as a whole.

reading:
The operator name on this row, News-Press and Gazette Company, is the name of the buyer at the moment of a transaction rather than the name the building trades under. NPG is a privately held media company based in St. Joseph, Missouri, owned by the Bradley family and known for newspapers, radio and television stations across the western United States. On 5 November 2018 it acquired Nebraska Data Centers, an Omaha interconnection business, through a newly formed entity called 1623 Farnam LLC, committing more than 30 million dollars of capital improvements over the following five years and retaining the existing president, Todd Cushing, to run it. The Bradley family subsequently sold most of NPG's traditional media assets and holds continuing investments through a separate vehicle, BERKS Group, so ultimate control has stayed within one family while the corporate wrapper around the data centre has changed. Anyone matching this row against a media company's own disclosures will not find the building, and that mismatch is the point of the entry.

The asset itself is 1623 Farnam Street in downtown Omaha, a nine storey building of roughly 75,000 square feet run as a carrier neutral interconnection hub rather than as a single tenant enterprise site. Its value is measured in cross connects rather than in floor space. It houses the Omaha Internet Exchange, operates as a certified Microsoft Azure ExpressRoute partner with direct cloud on ramps, and serves as a backhaul aggregation point for regional wireless and broadband operators, including the Iowa Communications Network, which joined the exchange there to extend statewide reach. The operator's current material says more than 60 network carriers are present, while its January 2026 expansion announcement describes the original location as connecting more than 50 network companies and reaching more than five million people across the region. Both counts are recorded rather than averaged.

The capacity record is partial and needs stating precisely. An expansion completed in mid 2025 added 1.5 megawatts of IT capacity and 280 new cabinets across the building's final two data halls, following a buildout in 2019 and additional floors brought into service in 2021. Reporting at the time put the resulting total at roughly 8 megawatts. The 1.5 megawatt figure is explicitly IT capacity. No utility service size, standby generator rating or on site fuel reserve has been published for the building. On 19 January 2026 the company announced it had closed on a second Omaha interconnection facility, to be operational in mid 2028 with at least 5 megawatts, described by chief executive Bill Severn as the next edge interconnection hub for the region.

One well sourced tenancy detail sits on the record. In February 2025 Fortune reported, on the basis of a footnote in a contract between Trump Media and Technology Group and the vendor WorldConnect Technologies, that the Omaha facility hosts a Truth Social data centre that became operational around August 2024, noting that Trump Media redacts such facility references from its own filings. That is recorded here as reported, with its sourcing named, and without further characterisation.

One registry side caution applies. The stored OpenStreetMap record for this row carries a postcode that belongs to a midtown Omaha delivery area rather than the downtown one covering that stretch of Farnam Street. The stored coordinates land within a couple of blocks of the building, so the tagging error is in the postcode field and not in the position.
